slides.title: Why data decisions come before network decisions
slides.notes: Ask: if your model has never seen rain, what does it say on a rainy day? It says something confident. That is the danger.

runs.text: Why data decisions come before network decisions
A network knows only what it saw
A delivery-time model trained on lunch orders near the kitchen has never seen an 8 pm order across the city. It will still answer, and it will be wrong.
More neurons, a better optimiser or longer training cannot add information that was never collected.
This is where the hours go
In industry projects most of the effort is collecting, cleaning and checking data. Training itself is often minutes.
A network interpolates between its examples. It does not know what lies outside them.

slides.title: Selection of data: cover the whole input space
slides.notes: Each input alone can look covered (all hours, all distances) while the far-and-late corner is empty. Coverage is about combinations.

runs.text: Selection of data: cover the whole input space
Delivery orders in the training set
6 am  →  hour of the day  →  midnight
Teal: situations with training orders.  Pink: no data, the model guesses.
The data must span every situation the network will meet
List the inputs and the range each one takes in real use.
Check every combination that matters, not each input alone.
A random sample of real use is the safest way to get coverage.
Empty regions cannot be seen in the error figures: the test set is blind in the same places.

slides.title: How much data is enough?
slides.notes: Hagan is explicit: the amount of data needed cannot be known before training. This links forward to L38 to L40.

runs.text: A smooth relationship needs few points. One with many bends (rush hours, weekends, rain) needs many. Noisy measurements need more again.
A 2-8-1 network has 33 weights and biases. With 40 examples it can memorise them. Aim for several examples for every weight.
There is no formula in advance. Post-training analysis tells you: if training error is low and test error is high, you needed more data or a smaller network.
Start with what you have, train, analyse, then decide whether to collect more.

slides.title: Divide the data three ways
slides.notes: Analogy: training set is the textbook exercises, validation is the model paper you use to decide when you are ready, test is the SEE itself.

runs.text: Computes the gradient and updates the weights
Decides when to stop and which network to keep
Never used in training. The honest final estimate
Each set answers a different question
70 / 15 / 15 is a common starting split, not a law.
Divide at random so all three sets cover the same situations.
If the test set influenced any decision, it is no longer a test.
For time series, divide in blocks of time, not at random.

slides.title: Normalisation: put every input on the same scale
slides.notes: Work one example on the board: distance from 200 m to 12,000 m, a 6,100 m order maps to 0. Then ask what an input of 15,000 m becomes: beyond +1, a sign of extrapolation.

runs.text: Normalisation: put every input on the same scale
First: min-max, maps each input to [−1, 1]. Second: mean and standard deviation, gives mean 0 and spread 1.
Compute min, max, mean and std from the training set only.
Store them. The same numbers must be applied to every new input after launch.
Normalise the targets too, then convert the output back to real units.
Mean and std is safer when a few extreme values would stretch min-max.

slides.title: Why scale? A sigmoid only responds near zero
slides.notes: This is the same saturation argument used later for weight initialisation in L37. Plant it now.

runs.text: Why scale? A sigmoid only responds near zero
Outside about −2 to 2 the neuron is flat
Distance in metres gives n in the thousands: every neuron sits pinned at +1.
A pinned neuron has almost zero slope, so the gradient is almost zero and learning stalls.
Large-valued inputs also dominate small ones (metres against hours).
Scaling changes nothing in the network. It changes what the network can learn.

slides.title: Beyond scaling: give the network better inputs
slides.notes: PCA: keep components that together explain, say, 98% of the variance. Caution: PCA is linear and ignores the targets, so check the result still predicts well.

runs.text: Beyond scaling: give the network better inputs
Use what you know. Take the log of income or price. Code the hour as sine and cosine so that 11 pm and 1 am sit close together.
Replace raw signals with a few meaningful numbers: from an ECG trace, the intervals and peak heights; from a vibration signal, the energy in each frequency band.
When inputs are many and correlated, rotate to uncorrelated components and keep those that carry most of the variance. Fewer inputs, fewer weights.
Every input removed means fewer weights to learn from the same data.

slides.title: Coding the targets
slides.notes: One-of-N is also called one-hot. The ±0.76 advice is from Hagan: it is where the tansig second derivative is largest.

rows.text: The value itself, normalised like the inputs
Linear output neuron can produce any value
Reads as the probability of class 1
One-of-N: N outputs, 1 for the right class, 0 elsewhere
No false ordering between classes; pairs with softmax
Targets of ±1 push the neuron into saturation

runs.text: Do not code classes as 1, 2, 3 on one neuron: that tells the network class 2 lies between 1 and 3.

slides.title: Missing data
slides.notes: The flag input lets the network learn that a missing value is itself informative, for example a sensor that drops out when it overheats.

runs.text: Drop the incomplete records. Check first that they are not all from one situation, or you create a blind spot.
Replace it with the mean of that input, and add an extra 0 / 1 input that flags "this value was missing".
Keep the record, but leave that output out of the error so it does not pull the weights.
Also remove records that are plainly wrong: a delivery that "took" 9 hours because nobody tapped Delivered.

slides.title: A classifier that fails in front of the class
slides.notes: Keep the failure on screen for a moment before fixing. The lesson is that the fix was a data fix.

In Teachable Machine, train "pen" against "phone" using only one student, one background, one angle.
